passage:
First Saturday: Pema told her parents she was at biology coaching. Instead she sat in Gopika's garage in Gangtok, painting prayer flags fluttering over a valley. Her hands were steady, but her stomach churned with guilt. Ama had saved for that coaching.
Two weeks later: The coaching centre called home. Ama's face was pale with hurt. "You lied to us." Pema wanted to shout that she hated biology, or just go silent and give up painting forever. She did neither. She said, "Can we talk tomorrow, when we're both calm?"
The next evening: At the kitchen table, Pema showed her parents her paintings. "I love you, and I know you want me safe. I want to try for the art college. Can I finish biology and do one art course alongside?" Pala looked at the valley painting for a long time. "Let's find out about both," he said.

qa.q: What did Pema paint in Gopika's garage?
qa.a: Prayer flags fluttering over a valley.

qa.q: How did Pema feel while painting instead of going to coaching?
qa.a: She felt guilty; her hands were steady but her stomach churned because Ama had saved for the coaching.

qa.q: Which choice helped Pema most, and why?
qa.a: Asking to talk when both were calm, then showing her paintings and proposing to do biology and one art course, which was open conversation instead of lying or giving up.

qa.q: How did Ama feel when the coaching centre called?
qa.a: Ama was hurt, her face pale, feeling lied to by Pema.

grounding: Shows a teen torn between family expectations of science and her love of art, moving from secret rebellion to open conversation.

subtype: Parent facing the child's different values [Receiver]
passage:
I still remember the evening, two years ago now, when Karthik put his engineering entrance forms on the table and said, "Appa, I don't want to do this. I want to study music."
My first feeling was fear. I thought of rent, of relatives asking questions, of him struggling at thirty. Then something like grief, for the future I had imagined for him since he was small. I almost said, "No, and that's final."
Instead I said, "Tell me why."
He talked for an hour. About how he felt most himself at the veena. About his teacher saying he had a real ear. About a music college with a teaching diploma, so he could earn.
I didn't agree that night. But I listened. Last month I watched him play at a sabha, eyes closed, and I felt a pride so strong it surprised me.
Shankar

qa.q: What instrument does Karthik play?
qa.a: The veena.

qa.q: What did Shankar feel when Karthik said he wanted to study music?
qa.a: He felt fear about money and Karthik's future, and grief for the future he had imagined for his son.

qa.q: What did Shankar do that kept the relationship intact?
qa.a: He asked "Tell me why" and listened for an hour before responding, instead of saying no straight away.

qa.q: How might Karthik have felt when his father asked "Tell me why"?
qa.a: Karthik probably felt nervous but relieved and taken seriously, which let him explain his reasons, including the teaching diploma.

grounding: Shows a father facing his son's choice of music over engineering, feeling fear, grief and later pride, and choosing to listen first.

passage:
In the college placement office in Indore, Sahil held the offer letter from the animation studio in Pune. His hands were shaking.
"You don't look happy," said Neelam, the placement officer.
"My father expects me to join the family's hardware shop. My grandfather started it. My brother is already there." He rubbed his face. "They paid for all this. I'm grateful. But I also feel angry that nobody asked what I want."
Neelam nodded. "Both can be true. What would honour the shop without giving up your own life?"
Sahil thought. "Maybe I could redo their signboard and set up their online orders. And come home every festival. And tell Papa about Pune myself, not by phone."
"That sounds like a start," Neelam said.
He folded the letter carefully into his pocket and booked a bus home for Sunday.

qa.q: Where was the animation studio that offered Sahil a job?
qa.a: In Pune.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel about his family's expectations?
qa.a: He felt grateful that they paid for his studies, and also angry and frustrated that nobody asked what he wanted.

qa.q: What path did Sahil come up with that honours both his roots and his own life?
qa.a: Helping the shop with a new signboard and online orders, coming home every festival, and telling his father about Pune in person.

qa.q: How might Sahil's father see the news about Pune?
qa.a: His father may feel hurt or worried, since he expected Sahil to join the shop, but hearing it in person with offers of help may make it easier to accept.

grounding: Shows a young adult torn between a job in another city and family custom, feeling gratitude and frustration, and seeking a path that honours both.

passage:
Chinmay, you asked why I've gone so quiet, so here it is. I'm Thomas, and I have two offers on my desk.
One is the bank clerk post. Permanent, pension, my parents already telling the whole parish. The other is a small studio making educational games, three people and a lot of hope.
I lie awake. One fear says: what if the studio shuts in a year and I've thrown away a safe job? The other fear says: what if I'm fifty and still wondering?
So I'm trying something small. I asked the studio if I could work with them on weekends for two months while I decide. They said yes. I'll see if I still love it when it's tiring and unpaid.
And I asked the bank for their latest joining date. It's in October. That gives me time to test before I choose.

qa.q: How many people work at the games studio?
qa.a: Three people.

qa.q: What is Thomas afraid of while lying awake?
qa.a: Thomas is afraid of losing a secure job if the studio shuts, and also afraid of being fifty and still wondering about the life not lived.

qa.q: Why is Thomas's weekend experiment a wise step?
qa.a: It tests the creative path in real conditions before giving up the secure job, with the October joining date giving time to decide.

qa.q: How might Thomas's parents see the choice?
qa.a: Thomas's parents are proud of the permanent post and already telling the parish, so they may feel worried if Thomas chooses the risky studio.

grounding: Shows a graduate weighing a secure job against a risky creative path, caught between two fears and testing the choice with a small experiment.

subtype: Observing a friend caught between worlds [Observer]
passage:
Every evening Asif waited for the last bus back from the district college with Vinita. This month, she had changed.
She used to chatter about her teaching course and the school she wanted to start in their village. Now she dozed against the window, dark circles under her eyes. When he asked how the wedding talks at home were going, she said, "Fine," and looked away.
Asif noticed she'd missed two assignments. He also noticed her mother calling three times a day.
One evening, as the bus bumped past the sugarcane fields, he said, "You don't have to tell me anything. But if you want to think out loud, I'll just listen. No advice."
She was quiet for a long time. Then: "They want me married by winter. I want to finish the course. I don't know how to hold both."
Asif nodded and said nothing, and she kept talking until their stop.

qa.q: What did Vinita want to start in their village?
qa.a: A school.

qa.q: How did Asif feel as he watched Vinita change?
qa.a: He was concerned for her, noticing how tired and evasive she had become, and wanted to help without pushing.

qa.q: Why did Asif's offer to just listen work?
qa.a: It gave Vinita space to think aloud without being pulled toward either her family's plan or her course, so she could speak freely.

qa.q: What is it like for Vinita to be caught between wedding plans and her course?
qa.a: She is exhausted and torn, not knowing how to hold both, which shows in her dozing, missed assignments and short answers.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing a tired, evasive peer caught between family expectations and her goals, and offering to listen without taking sides.

subtype: Loyalty to family versus honesty with self [Actor]
passage:
Every month, on the first, Irfan transferred most of his salary home from his Bengaluru office. Abbu's shop had closed during the lockdown, and his younger sister, Dilnaz, was in college.
He loved them. He was proud he could do it. But the design course he'd wanted for three years was still just a saved link. He'd skipped his friend's wedding in Goa to save the fare.
Last Sunday, on the video call, Ammi said, "Beta, the neighbour's son bought a car."
Irfan felt something hot rise in his chest, then immediately felt guilty for it.
After the call, Dilnaz messaged him. "Bhaiya, you look tired. Are you okay?"
He typed and deleted three times. Then: "I love helping. But I need to keep some for myself too. I want to do my course. Can we talk to Ammi and Abbu together about what's possible?"
Dilnaz replied: "Yes. I'll be there."

qa.q: What did Irfan skip to save the fare?
qa.a: His friend's wedding in Goa.

qa.q: What did Irfan feel when Ammi mentioned the neighbour's son's car?
qa.a: He felt a flash of resentment, something hot rising in his chest, and then felt guilty for it.

qa.q: What step did Irfan take toward being honest with himself and his family?
qa.a: He told Dilnaz he needed to keep something for himself and his course, and asked to talk to their parents together about what's possible.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel reading Irfan's message?
qa.a: Dilnaz, who noticed he looked tired, may feel relieved he was honest and glad to support him by being there for the talk.

grounding: Shows a young adult supporting his family while delaying his own wants, feeling both love and resentment, and moving toward a clear talk about limits.

passage:
In her small Vancouver kitchen, Chen laid two sticky notes on the table. One said: Toronto promotion. The other: Nai Nai.
Her friend Valentina poured tea. "Talk me through it."
"The promotion protects my career, my growth, the thing I've worked for." Chen touched the second note. "Staying protects my time with my grandmother. She's eighty-nine."
"So what does each one really guard?"
"Growth. And love, time I can't get back."
They sat with it. Then Chen said, "What if I ask to start the role remotely for six months? Fly to Toronto once a month. Then decide about moving."
"And if they say no?"
Chen breathed out. "Then I'll choose Nai Nai, and I'll grieve the job. I won't pretend it doesn't cost anything."
She opened her laptop and began drafting the email to her manager.

qa.q: What did the two sticky notes say?
qa.a: Toronto promotion, and Nai Nai.

qa.q: How does Chen feel about possibly losing the promotion?
qa.a: Chen feels sad and ready to grieve the job, accepting that the choice has a real cost.

qa.q: Which steps in Chen's thinking could help others facing a values conflict?
qa.a: She named each value, asked what each protects, looked for a sequence like starting remotely that honours both, and accepted some loss either way.

qa.q: What would change if Chen pretended the choice cost nothing?
qa.a: She might feel confused or resentful later, because an unnamed loss can linger; naming it lets her decide clearly.

grounding: Shows a young adult naming competing values, asking what each protects, seeking a sequence that honours both, and accepting some loss.

passage:
The whole family had arrived for Diwali, and the house was loud with cousins, crackers and pressure cookers. Rukmini sat in the corner with her goal chart: 50 physics problems by Sunday, 45 done.
She'd hit every target this term. When she didn't have one, she felt restless and bored, pacing the room.
Her phone buzzed. Varun: "you coming to my birthday thing tonight?? you said yes last week"
She'd forgotten. Again. That made it three missed plans this month.
Rukmini stared at the chart. Five problems left. Her chest tightened; stopping felt like failing.
Her cousin Leela peeked in. "Are you ever just happy, didi? Or only when you finish?"
Rukmini didn't answer. Then, slowly, she put the chart down, typed "coming, 20 mins," and went to find a clean kurta. The five problems could wait until tomorrow.

qa.q: How many physics problems had Rukmini done by the time Varun messaged?
How did Rukmini feel when she thought about stopping?
qa.a: She felt tense and uneasy, with her chest tightening, because stopping felt like failing.

qa.q: What did Rukmini risk by focusing only on her targets?
qa.a: She risked her friendships, having missed three plans this month, and making success the only measure of her worth.

qa.q: How might Varun feel if Rukmini missed his birthday too?
qa.a: Varun might feel hurt and unimportant, since she had said yes last week and had already missed other plans.

grounding: Shows a goal-driven teen who feels restless without targets, and who starts to notice friendships slipping when success is all that counts.

passage:
The hostel corridor was never quiet: music, arguments, someone always frying eggs. Eshaan sat on his bed with the tabla, practising the same eight-beat pattern for the hundredth time, slowly.
His cousin Ayesha, visiting for the weekend, watched. "You're not even in the college band. Why not audition? Or post videos, get followers?"
Eshaan shrugged. "I'm not ready."
"You've been saying that for two years. Don't you want to be somebody?"
He smiled a little. "I want to be good. Really good. That's the goal."
He didn't tell her he'd written it in a notebook: clean tirakita at full speed by December. He didn't tell anyone. Some people thought he lacked drive. He didn't mind much.
That night, through the noise, he played the pattern twice at full speed without a single mistake. He grinned to himself, and started again.

qa.q: What did Eshaan write as his goal in the notebook?
qa.a: Clean tirakita at full speed by December.

qa.q: How did Eshaan feel when he played the pattern cleanly at full speed?
qa.a: He felt quietly pleased and satisfied, grinning to himself before starting again.

qa.q: What might help others understand Eshaan's kind of ambition?
qa.a: Asking about his private goals, like the notebook target, instead of judging his drive by auditions or followers.

qa.q: How does Ayesha see Eshaan's practice?
qa.a: Ayesha misreads it as a lack of drive, since he isn't auditioning or posting, and doesn't know about his private goal.

grounding: Shows a young adult with quiet, mastery-focused ambition whose private, steady goals are misread by a cousin as lack of drive.

passage:
Dear Nandini Di,
You asked how it feels to finally be at the top college everyone at home talks about. I've been putting off replying, because the honest answer is: empty.
I chased it for four years. Rank 212. The name on my hoodie. Papa showing the admission letter to every uncle. For a week I felt amazing. Then it faded, and now I'm already worrying about getting the "right" internship with the "right" title.
Last night I asked myself something you once asked me: whose applause am I working for? Mostly Papa's. Some of it for the boys in my old coaching batch.
I don't know what I want instead yet. But I remember loving the electronics club in Class 9, building a radio that actually worked. Nobody clapped for that. I was just happy.
Maybe I'll start there.
Vishal

qa.q: What rank did Vishal get?
qa.a: Rank 212.

qa.q: How does Vishal feel now about reaching the top college?
qa.a: Vishal feels empty and hollow, after only a week of feeling amazing, and is already worrying about the next title.

qa.q: What question is helping Vishal redirect ambition?
qa.a: "Whose applause am I working for?", which shows it is mostly for Papa and old classmates, and points back to the electronics club Vishal loved.

qa.q: How might Nandini feel reading this email?
qa.a: Nandini may feel moved and glad that Vishal is being honest and using the question Nandini once asked.

grounding: Shows a student who chased ranks and titles for others' approval, feels hollow on reaching them, and reflects on whose approval drives the ambition.
